strengths: Addresses a fundamental and prevalent challenge in spectral imaging: the inability of existing models to generalize across cameras with varying numbers of spectral channels and differing wavelength band sensitivities.

Well-formulated architectural design: combining continuous Fourier wavelength positional encodings with a query-based cross-attention compression mechanism allows the model to map arbitrary spectral configurations into fixed-dimensional camera-agnostic representations.
A coherent self-supervised pre-training framework (CARL-SSL) extending the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to both spectral and spatial dimensions with VICReg regularization.

Extensive empirical validation across three distinct domains (medical porcine organ segmentation, automotive urban scene understanding, and Earth observation land cover classification), demonstrating consistent gains over camera-specific models and recent channel-adaptive baselines (e.g., Hyve, HyperFree, Spectral Adapter, and SpectralGPT+).

Detailed analysis of computational complexity, showing that the query cross-attention design scales linearly with spectral channels and reduces FLOPs substantially compared to 3D spatio-spectral attention models like SpectralGPT+.
weaknesses: While the overall system is novel in its domain, the core architectural components (continuous Fourier feature embeddings, Perceiver-style query cross-attention, and I-JEPA / VICReg objectives) are adaptations of established methods in general vision and representation learning.

In the remote sensing evaluation (Table 2), pre-training modalities differ significantly: baselines like SpectralGPT+ and SatMAE pre-train on over 700k–1M MSI images, whereas CARL-SSL pre-trains on 11k HSI images (202 bands). While the data efficiency claim is valid in terms of image count, the qualitative difference in spectral information during pre-training makes direct attribution between architecture vs. data richness slightly ambiguous.

Ablations could be expanded to dissect the SSL components, such as isolating the specific impact of the spectral predictor vs. spatial predictor, as well as the sensitivity to the spectral masking ratio.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in spectral imaging: the incompatibility of models across different sensors with varying channel dimensions, filter bandwidths, and spectral ranges (RGB, MSI, and HSI).

Principled architectural formulation: using continuous Fourier feature wavelength positional encodings allows handling arbitrary spectral bands without discrete tokenization, while learned query representations effectively compress the spectral dimension prior to spatial transformer processing.

Novel and effective self-supervised pre-training scheme (CARL-SSL) adapting the JEPA framework with VICReg loss to jointly learn spectral and spatial representations in feature space without relying on pixel reconstruction.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across three distinct domains (porcine organ segmentation, urban autonomous driving scene parsing, and remote sensing land cover classification), demonstrating consistent gains over strong baselines like HyperFree, Hyve, Spectral Adapter, and SpectralGPT+.
Compelling demonstration of cross-modality knowledge transfer, such as transferring semantic knowledge of unannotated HSI classes ('poles') directly from RGB Cityscapes data.
weaknesses: In the medical proof-of-concept benchmark (Section 4.1), spectral variation is synthetically created via idealized Gaussian filter convolutions over existing HSI data, which simplifies real-world optical variations such as sensor noise, quantum efficiency curves, and lighting discrepancies.

While significantly more computationally efficient than 3D patch models like SpectralGPT+ (120.5G vs 242.1G FLOPs), CARL incurs noticeably higher FLOP overhead compared to spatial-only adapter baselines like Hyve and HyperFree (~6.4G FLOPs), which warrants further discussion regarding real-time deployment constraints.

In the ViT-Adapter hierarchical feature extraction (Section A.1), only a single channel is fed into the spatial convolutions to maintain channel invariance; the specific channel selection criterion and its sensitivity/impact on spatial feature quality are not thoroughly analyzed.

Pre-training dataset comparisons in Table 2 involve inherently different data distributions and resolutions (HySpecNet-11k HSI vs. large-scale MSI), making it difficult to fully isolate the algorithmic benefits of CARL-SSL from the informational density of the pre-training modality.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and long-standing challenge in spectral imaging: the inability of conventional vision models to handle varying channel counts and heterogeneous wavelength bands across different sensors (RGB, multispectral, and hyperspectral).

The proposed architecture is well-designed and conceptually elegant: by using continuous Fourier feature positional encodings for wavelengths and a query-based cross-attention mechanism to compress arbitrary spectral bands into fixed-size representations, the method achieves genuine channel-dimension invariance.

The introduction of CARL-SSL, an end-to-end JEPA-based self-supervised framework operating jointly in spectral and spatial feature spaces with VICReg regularization, provides a sensible, pixel-reconstruction-free pre-training scheme for heterogeneous spectral data.

Evaluation spans three diverse application domains (medical organ segmentation, autonomous driving scene segmentation, and satellite remote sensing), demonstrating clear empirical gains over existing channel-adaptive baselines (such as Hyve, HyperFree, and Spectral Adapter) and foundation models (SpectralGPT+).
weaknesses: Backbone consistency in baseline comparisons: In the medical imaging experiment (Section 4.1), the camera-specific model and Hyve use a U-Net backbone, while HyperFree and Spectral Adapter use ViT and EVA-02 backbones. Disentangling the benefits of the spectral encoder from the underlying spatial architecture would require strictly matching backbones across all comparisons.

Omission of spectral response functions (SRFs) / bandwidth: The spectral positional encoding only conditions on the center wavelength $\lambda_i$. In practice, broad-band multispectral and RGB filters have significantly different bandwidths (FWHM) and response curves compared to narrow-band hyperspectral sensors. Relying solely on scalar center wavelengths may limit representation fidelity when bridging RGB and HSI.

Heuristic channel selection in ViT-Adapter: For hierarchical feature generation (Section A.1), the authors state that 'a single channel of the given spectral image was used as input to these convolutions'. It is not clearly specified how this single channel is selected across different modalities, nor whether discarding the remaining channels for the spatial adapter degrades fine-grained spatial-spectral feature extraction.

The aggregation of learned queries into the spatial representation relies on an unweighted summation ($\sum Q_j$). While simple, an ablation or justification of this pooling operation over learned projection or attention pooling is missing.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in spectral imaging: learning representations that generalize across heterogeneous camera configurations with varying channel counts and wavelength specifications.

Well-motivated and novel architecture that decouples spectral distillation (via learnable spectral queries cross-attending to wavelength-encoded spectral tokens) from standard spatial transformer backbones, achieving channel invariance while capturing inter-band spectral relationships.

Novel feature-based self-supervised learning framework (CARL-SSL) combining masked spectral token prediction with spatial I-JEPA and VICReg regularization, avoiding the sensitivity of pixel-level reconstruction in spectral data.

Comprehensive and diverse empirical evaluation spanning three distinct domains (medical imaging, autonomous driving, and satellite Earth observation), demonstrating superior cross-sensor transfer, robustness to spectral variations, and cross-modality zero-shot label transfer.
Extensive ablations and analyses, including variance decomposition, t-SNE clustering across modalities, SSL component contributions, and FLOP complexity comparisons.
weaknesses: Higher computational footprint compared to lightweight channel-adaptive projection methods (e.g., DOFA at 8.0 GFLOPs vs. CARL at 120.5 GFLOPs), since spectral cross-attention is computed for every spatial patch independently.

Downstream performance margins over the strongest baseline (DOFA) in remote sensing benchmarks (e.g., SegMunich fine-tuning and linear probing) are relatively modest (1.4 mIoU and 0.7 mIoU, respectively).

To manage GPU memory, the model randomly subsamples channels (down to 32 during training and 64 during pretraining); the effect of this subsampling on high-resolution spectral signature resolution deserves more discussion.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in spectral imaging: the inability of existing architectures and foundation models to seamlessly handle varying channel counts and heterogeneous wavelength specifications across different camera sensors.

The technical design is elegant and sound: combining continuous wavelength Fourier positional encodings with a cross-attention distillation mechanism (using K learnable queries) enables channel-invariant, camera-agnostic spatio-spectral representation learning.

The self-supervised pre-training strategy (CARL-SSL) is well-motivated and technically justified: feature-level prediction of masked spectral channels regularized by VICReg effectively prevents representation collapse, as convincingly shown in the ablation study (Table 3c).

Comprehensive and diverse empirical evaluation spanning three distinct application domains (medical organ segmentation, automotive scene understanding, and earth observation / remote sensing) with simulated and real-world sensor shifts.
Thorough ablation studies verifying key design choices, including positional encoding parameters, aggregation strategies, query token count K, and individual loss terms.
weaknesses: Higher computational complexity than channel-adaptive spatial-only baselines (e.g., DOFA, Hyve), as executing spectral cross-attention per spatial patch increases FLOPs significantly (120.5G vs ~8.0G on 128x128x48 inputs), although it remains more efficient than dense 3D patch models like SpectralGPT+.

To manage GPU memory during training, random subsampling of spectral channels (to 32 or 64 channels) is required when processing dense hyperspectral cubes, reflecting potential memory bottlenecks for high-resolution hyperspectral inputs.
On certain remote sensing linear probing benchmarks (e.g., m-cashew-plantation in Table 4), the performance improvement over strong baselines like DOFA is marginal.

strengths: Compelling and important problem formulation: addressing channel dimensionality and wavelength heterogeneity across spectral imaging modalities (RGB, multispectral, hyperspectral) to break down camera-specific data silos.

Well-designed and principled architecture: combining continuous Fourier wavelength positional encodings with a self-attention/cross-attention bottleneck distills variable-channel inputs into a fixed number of learned spectral tokens, ensuring camera-agnostic processing for downstream spatial encoders.

Novel spatio-spectral self-supervised pre-training (CARL-SSL): successfully extends joint-embedding predictive architectures (I-JEPA) with feature-level spectral token masking and VICReg loss, preventing representation collapse and avoiding fragile pixel-level reconstruction.

Comprehensive, multi-domain evaluation: demonstrates robustness and cross-camera generalization across three diverse application domains (medical imaging, autonomous driving, and satellite remote sensing) on both synthetic and real-world sensor setups.

Strong empirical results and convincing baselines: consistently outperforms prior camera-agnostic and channel-adaptive methods (such as DOFA, Hyve, HyperFree, and Spectral Adapter) as well as camera-specific baselines.

Thorough ablations, analyses, and reproducibility: provides detailed ablations on architectural choices (PE parameters, token aggregation, number of tokens K), FLOPs analysis, semantic vs. sensor variance decomposition, and clean algorithmic pseudo-code.
weaknesses: Increased computational overhead compared to purely spatial projection baselines: processing per-patch spectral cross-attention introduces noticeably higher FLOP counts than lightweight projection-based methods like DOFA or Hyve (though substantially lower than full spatio-spectral attention models like SpectralGPT+).

Simplifying assumption on spectral bands: the wavelength positional encoding relies solely on center wavelengths and does not explicitly incorporate spectral bandwidths (filter response curves / full-width half-maximum), which can vary significantly between narrow hyperspectral bands and broad RGB/multispectral bands.

Training-time channel subsampling: due to memory constraints on single GPUs, the model relies on subsampling to 32 or 64 channels during training, leaving questions about potential scalability limits when scaling to hundreds of raw channels simultaneously without subsampling.

Incremental gains on certain satellite benchmarks: while performance gains are substantial on m-forestnet and m-SA-crop-type, improvements on tasks such as m-cashew-plantation and linear probe SegMunich are relatively marginal over DOFA.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: overcoming sensor-specific data silos caused by varying channel counts and spectral response curves across RGB, multispectral, and hyperspectral imaging.

Well-motivated architecture: decoupling spectral and spatial processing via wavelength positional encoding and a cross-attention bottleneck into fixed learnable tokens allows flexible handling of arbitrary channel configurations while explicitly modeling cross-channel dependencies.

Novel SSL framework (CARL-SSL): successfully extends feature-based self-supervised learning (JEPA/VICReg) into the spectral domain, circumventing noisy pixel-level reconstructions that commonly plague spectral imaging.

Extensive cross-domain benchmarking: tested across three distinct domains (medical imaging, autonomous driving, and remote sensing) on both synthetic/controlled and real-world out-of-distribution sensors, demonstrating consistent superiority over strong recent baselines like DOFA, Copernicus-FM, and SpectralGPT.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: includes detailed ablations on architectural choices (PE variance, aggregation, number of spectral tokens), a clear complexity/FLOPs analysis, pseudo-code algorithms, and feature variance decomposition showing strong invariance to sensor confounding.
weaknesses: Computational cost: While substantially more efficient than 3D attention approaches like SpectralGPT, CARL still exhibits higher FLOPs than purely spatial channel-adaptive projection methods (e.g., DOFA) as channel counts increase (e.g., on 116-channel hyperspectral data).

Adapter design for dense prediction: For high-resolution dense prediction, the method feeds a single channel into the ViT-Adapter convolutional branches to preserve channel-invariance, which might discard subtle high-frequency spatial details that only appear in specific spectral bands.

Pre-training compute and dataset scale: In remote sensing, pre-training is carried out on an H200 GPU on a subset of SpectralEarth and BigEarthNet; exploring scaling laws with larger pre-training sets would further strengthen the claims regarding foundation model capabilities.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in spectral imaging: the inability of existing models to generalize seamlessly across sensors with varying channel dimensions, spectral coverages, and modalities (RGB, MSI, and HSI).

Novel and elegant architectural design: combining continuous wavelength Fourier positional encodings with a patch-level self-attention and cross-attention mechanism into a fixed number of learned spectral queries enables genuine camera-agnostic spatio-spectral encoding.

First feature-based spatio-spectral self-supervised pre-training framework (CARL-SSL) combining spatial masking (I-JEPA) with spectral token masking regularized by VICReg loss, effectively preventing spectral representation collapse.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across three distinct domains (medical imaging, autonomous driving, and Earth observation), demonstrating superior cross-sensor transfer and out-of-distribution robustness compared to both camera-specific and existing channel-adaptive foundation models.

Clear, detailed ablation studies validating core architectural choices (continuous wavelength positional encoding, number of queries K, aggregation strategies, and the necessity of spectral self-supervision).
weaknesses: Increased computational cost: because the spectral encoder operates on each spatial patch independently, computing attention across spectral channels incurs non-trivial FLOP overhead compared to purely spatial projection approaches (e.g., DOFA), particularly as the channel count grows large (e.g., Gaofen-5).

The medical validation relies primarily on a private porcine dataset with synthetic/filter-simulated multispectral images rather than evaluations on diverse real-world medical camera hardware across different institutions.

The pre-training scale in satellite imaging (~800k samples) is relatively modest compared to recent multi-million-scale Earth observation foundation models, though the comparative benchmarking against existing models is fair and solid.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in spectral image analysis: learning representations that generalize across cameras with varying channel counts and spectral sensitivities without requiring camera-specific retraining.

Well-motivated and sound technical approach: the combination of continuous Fourier wavelength positional encodings, patch-wise spectral self-attention, and cross-attention distillation into a fixed set of learnable spectral representations cleanly decouples spectral and spatial encoding.

A novel spatio-spectral feature-based self-supervised learning strategy (CARL-SSL) combining masked spectral token prediction via VICReg with spatial I-JEPA pre-training, effectively circumventing the noise sensitivities inherent to pixel-level reconstruction in spectral data.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across three diverse domains: medical organ segmentation, urban scene perception (autonomous driving), and satellite remote sensing foundation models, covering both simulated and real-world cross-sensor variations.

Solid performance on zero-shot out-of-distribution sensor evaluation in remote sensing benchmarks (achieving an average rank of 1.6 across 11 datasets), as well as strong ablations isolating the importance of wavelength positional encoding, aggregation strategies, number of spectral tokens, and the dual SSL loss components.
weaknesses: Computational overhead: performing spectral self-attention across all channels for every spatial patch can scale significantly with image resolution and channel count, leading to higher GFLOPs than purely spatial projection baselines (as shown in Table 11 for Gaofen-5), though random channel subsampling partially alleviates this during training.

In-distribution performance trade-offs: on certain established remote sensing benchmarks such as m-eurosat (Table 4), CARL underperforms dedicated baselines like DOFA and SMARTIES (84.4% vs. 89.9% and 92.6%), suggesting that while cross-camera generalization is improved, there may be slight trade-offs on specific in-distribution tasks.

Reliance on band-independent 2D patch projection at the earliest stage may discard fine-grained local spectral-spatial interaction prior to the spectral attention module, which could be relevant for narrow absorption bands.

Parts of the automotive and medical validation rely on simulated multispectral generation from hyperspectral data or relatively small cohort sizes, although real-world filter validation and large-scale satellite evaluations mitigate this concern.
